title: Bhai Mani Singh at Damdama
hookLine: the scribe who wrote out the Granth as the Guru dictated, later granthi at the Harmandir

lines: A MAN WITH A REED PEN.
cards: After Muktsar, the Guru keeps moving, and tradition says he comes to rest at Talwandi Sabo, in the dry Malwa country. Sikhs know the place as Damdama Sahib. For a while there is no siege, no pursuit.

And the Guru turns to something that has nothing to do with swords. He begins to recite. Beside him sits a man with ink, a reed pen and a great stack of paper, writing down every line, carefully, as it comes.

teach.b: Here is what Sikh tradition says happened at Damdama. Guru Gobind Singh recited the scripture, the Granth that Guru Arjan had compiled, and Bhai Mani Singh wrote it out as he dictated.

Into this version, tradition says, the Guru added the hymns of his father, Guru Tegh Bahadur. Sikhs remember this as the version of the Granth that the Guru later named as Guru, the Guru Granth Sahib.
So look at what Bhai Mani Singh was doing. Not composing. Not editing to his taste.

teach.h: A SCRIBE STAYS OUT OF THE WAY.
teach.b: Listening, and writing exactly what he heard, line after line, day after day, without letting his own voice creep in. A scribe's whole skill is to stay out of the way. A careless hand can drop a word.
A proud hand can improve one. His job was to do neither. He had been near the Guru's household since boyhood, tradition says, and he stayed close for the rest of his life.
Later, tradition says, he was sent to Amritsar to serve as granthi at the Harmandir, the reader and keeper of the scripture there, at a hard and dangerous time for Sikhs.

Tradition says that years later, after a dispute with the Lahore authorities over a Diwali gathering of Sikhs at Amritsar, he was executed in Lahore, refusing to give up his faith to save his life, and he is remembered as a martyr.
But today belongs to the quieter years: the room at Damdama, the voice reciting, the pen moving. Sikhs sometimes call Damdama the Guru's Kashi, a place of learning.
In this telling, its learning starts with someone writing slowly and well.

how: Sikhs honor Takht Sri Damdama Sahib at Talwandi Sabo as the place where, tradition says, the Granth was written out with Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymns included, and they remember Bhai Mani Singh as scribe, granthi and martyr.

games.q: you're the scribe. the Guru is reciting, and one line seems to you like it could be said more beautifully. what do you do?
o: write it exactly as it was spoken.
leave it out and ask later.
games.why: a scribe's whole skill is to stay out of the way. tradition remembers Bhai Mani Singh writing exactly what he heard.

practice: Find a pen and paper and choose one line that matters to you: a line of Gurbani if you know one, like Ik Onkar, or a line from someone you love.
Write it out slowly, every letter, without improving or rushing it; when your mind wanders, return to the next letter. Then read it back once, exactly as written.
